## The passive-scalar limiter and the complement bound {#sec-ch08-scalar}

### Summary

Passive scalars are transported by the same divergence as the hydro species and are limited by the same
scheme. This section exists because the call is a separate one, in a separate module, with its own
counters, and a reader looking for it in the hydro path will not find it.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
- Passive scalars get the same limiter as the hydro species, from the same function.
- Switch: the same limiter switch; the scalar module runs its own call, which also runs whenever the scalar
  added its own covariance row (@sec-ch04-fluxcov).
- The factors are exchanged as a raw copy, never interpolated, for the same reason as the hydro ones.
- A scalar bounded above by its complement needs a second constraint, which is noted here, not derived.
:::

### Derivation

Nothing new: the derivation is @sec-ch08-theta, and the scalar module calls the same two functions. The
argument for the ghost exchange being a raw copy rather than an interpolation is also the same, and the
code comment points back to the hydro call site rather than repeating it.

The one thing specific to scalars is the upper bound. A scalar that represents a fraction is bounded
above by the positivity of its complement, so enforcing non-negativity on the scalar alone is not
enough to keep it below one. The code comment at `the` ({{< code src/scalar/scalar.cpp ScalarImpl::reset >}}) records this; the
chapter records it as a stated design intent and does not claim a derivation, because none is committed.

Because the derivation is @sec-ch08-theta's, so is its check: the guarantee `[C1]`, the inactivity away from
depletion `[C2]`, the face-cancellation argument `[C3]` and the donor rule `[C7]` are the same claims for the
scalar module, which calls the same two functions [check `src/snapy_report/ch08/positivity_check.py`, output
`src/snapy_report/ch08/positivity_check.out`]. The upper bound of the paragraph above is not among them: it has
no committed derivation to check.

### Numerical method

The call is `_flux1` ({{< code src/scalar/scalar.cpp ScalarImpl::forward >}}), which builds the factors with the same
`flux_positivity_theta`, counts the cells it limited, and scales through the synchronised factors. The
synchronisation is the lambda at `theta_opts` ({{< code src/scalar/scalar.cpp ScalarImpl::forward >}}): it puts the factors into a variable
map, exchanges them with interpolation switched off, and applies the physical boundary functions, which
is exactly the fill the limiter's contract requires.

The call runs when `limiter` is set or `cov` is
({{< code src/scalar/scalar.cpp ScalarImpl::forward >}}); the scalar sets `cov` when it added its own covariance row
({{< code src/scalar/scalar.cpp ScalarImpl::forward >}}), because that row can export tracer a cell does not hold, as for the hydro species
(@sec-ch08-theta).

### Tests

No test in the repository selects the passive-scalar limiter on its own. Its behaviour follows from
@sec-ch08-theta, whose checks cover the shared function. `test_scalar_flux_covariance` and
`test_scalar_cov_x1_split`
({{< code tests/CMakeLists.txt >}}) run passive scalars with `limiter: false` and the covariance on
(`limiter` in {{< code tests/test_scalar_flux_covariance.py config >}}), so their
covariance-on arms go through this call; they assert the scalar against the species and the split, not the
limiter's counters (@sec-ch04-fluxcov).

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- The upper bound is not enforced. The limiter keeps a scalar non-negative; nothing in this path keeps
  it below its complement, and the code comment describes that as the intent rather than the behaviour.
:::

1. **Untested path.** The two scalar covariance tests run the call, but no test asserts on its counters or its
   exchange, so those are written from reading alone.
